### 2026-10-09 – # October 9: Finished the Schematic

**2.5h**

# October 9: Finished the Schematic

![Screenshot 2026-10-09 at 10.54.50 PM](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/oWK9iPLBGiJtrZ5WPQtAnBOy06yuxWnK/71adad5c0bfc0669de9ada39591e053fe372c3077c9ab92913cb6d7893cfb5dd.png)

I finally finished the schematic for QuickPad, my six-key macropad with a screen that displays the date and time. I had initially designed a simple devboard, but I realized that it would be too expensive and too hard to solder, so now I'm switching to this! I'm using a Seeed XIAO RP2040 module, 6 mechanical keyboard switches, a 0.91 inch OLED display, and a DS3231 clock module so the macropad can tell the time, even when unplugged (I found this out while scrolling on Youtube a couple weeks ago. While planning for this project, I thought it would be a great addition!). While designing, I also decided to add a rotary encoder for volume control. This isn't the first time I've used KiCad, but it is my first time using it to design something entirely my own. After looking around online for some inspiration, making a macropad stuck out to me because my keyboard actually doesn't have function keys, which I recently found out are extremely helpful. I want to map the QuickPad's keys to specific function keys that I use for video games, shortcuts etc.

![Screenshot 2026-10-09 at 10.55.30 PM](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/oWK9iPLBGiJtrZ5WPQtAnBOy06yuxWnK/23e37b9a7cfa0e501b7eb57f90972a808e9c6162b1553b9594ad5d54852f34a9.png)
I got stuck trying to figure out how to add the footprints for the screen and clock module, but after searching it up, I found out that you can actually use headers as a stand-in for the actual modules, which makes sense because the screen and clock can simply be soldered in.

![Screenshot 2026-10-09 at 10.55.56 PM](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/oWK9iPLBGiJtrZ5WPQtAnBOy06yuxWnK/eecd588d4285a4ed2c5cd165c9a52a9c210c6f2cdd3133d5f45cb0cb97f6e097.png)

I also tried using labels for the first time in a KiCad project, which I found makes things a lot easier to make and understand.

![Screenshot 2026-10-09 at 10.55.43 PM](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/oWK9iPLBGiJtrZ5WPQtAnBOy06yuxWnK/23f3f8c1272904a4fd0f3eee88cdeb26f9bca082693211777bfbc00ccb980ce8.png)

The next step is routing the board!

# tl;dr: I finished the schematic for QuickPad, a six-key macropad with a screen to display date and time. I used labels for the first time and used header pins to represent an OLED screen and a time module.

### 2026-10-10 – # October 9-10: Shopping

**2h**

# October 9-10: Shopping

![Screenshot 2026-10-10 at 12.36.29 AM](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/oWK9iPLBGiJtrZ5WPQtAnBOy06yuxWnK/8109792424f8cdd80829b20cb009ce6344185b5ccbe20986ce0103da68537e9a.png)

I decided to skip around a little bit and look for some of the components I need online. I found a majority of the components I need on Amazon, including the OLED screen, the time module, and keycaps. I had to go to the Seeed website to find the RP2040 chip I need for my project. By this point, I realized that this bill of materials would exceed the $30 limit I would receive for a Tier 1 project. I tried looking around for cheaper substitutes, which led me to find a cheap pack of OLED screens and keycaps. However, I still exceeded the project budget. I thought I might have some extra components lying around my house and after searching my desk and my brother's room, I found a spare rotary encoder and more than enough switches. Next, I went to JLCPCB to check how much my board would cost to manufacture. With a coupon, it's only $1.13, but that might change because I haven't finished designing the board yet. But for the most part, my bill of materials is complete!

![Screenshot 2026-10-10 at 12.35.25 AM](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/oWK9iPLBGiJtrZ5WPQtAnBOy06yuxWnK/9025189894af769eadd76422a7b9e07a6925ef02e58eee545cf0e82d0354e055.png)

Tomorrow I'm going to work on finishing the PCB and getting starting with firmware and setting up my Github repo.

# tl;dr: I shopped for parts online. I already own switches and a rotary encoder, so all I needed to find was the XIAO RP2040, which I found on the Seeed store, and the OLED screen, keycaps, and the time module, which I found on Amazon.

### 2026-10-10 – # October 10: Finished Routing the PCB!

**4h**

# October 10: Finished Routing the PCB!

![Screenshot 2026-10-10 at 2.41.21 PM](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/oWK9iPLBGiJtrZ5WPQtAnBOy06yuxWnK/8f335af7c750652f410745af6ba33f6f7e83f77001695069b885cef44ee90991.png)

After a bit of trial and error work, I finally completed the PCB! Routing a board is a lot harder than I thought because you also have to consider where your traces are and what layers they are in, because they can't cross.  I had to redo my tracing a couple times because I ran into this problem.

The biggest obstacle I encountered while designing the board was an issue with the footprint of the RP2040 chip I was using. I double checked my schematic and the library I imported, but everything seemed fine. I took a closer look at the error, and realized it was a problem with the footprint. I had forgotten to add the footprint library! I went back to the Github repository where I downloaded the symbols library but I couldn't find the footprint library, so I had to manually search for it online. After I got it, I imported it into my project so I could route the PCB properly. Later, after routing the board, I realized that I had forgotten to flip the RP2040! That meant I had to reroute the board and essentially restart from scratch. It was kind of annoying and tedious, but I think my redesign came out better than the original because I was more precise with adding the footprints, especially for the switches.

![Screenshot 2026-10-10 at 2.41.57 PM](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/oWK9iPLBGiJtrZ5WPQtAnBOy06yuxWnK/947e213c15c26a3d71c323116ea6a677665cf9ebf3f48a572b182659f1864da9.png)

![Screenshot 2026-10-10 at 2.43.37 PM](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/oWK9iPLBGiJtrZ5WPQtAnBOy06yuxWnK/e313fefd8b31e2a4fbbe0eaa1c3a40bd6639ceb4e9614b9bc32da2cedab576f0.png)

![Screenshot 2026-10-10 at 2.44.12 PM](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/oWK9iPLBGiJtrZ5WPQtAnBOy06yuxWnK/1eaaf35442bab9e3d978fae2017fb99a87c33d462de802c3e8eb2d99be855b5c.png)

I'm nearly there, all I need to do now is the firmware and finalizing the Github repository.

# tl;dr: After encountering a problem with the footprint of the XIAO RP2040, I imported the footprint and continued working, but I had to reroute the board after realizing I hadn't flipped the RP2040.

### 2026-10-10 – # October 10: Making firmware and finalizing GitHub Repository

**3h**

# October 10: Making firmware and finalizing GitHub Repository

![Screenshot 2026-10-10 at 7.56.03 PM](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/oWK9iPLBGiJtrZ5WPQtAnBOy06yuxWnK/252211da18e0bb3154d791931726c618e3e0787bef07b5a9017c787378797857.png)

![Screenshot 2026-10-10 at 7.56.42 PM](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/oWK9iPLBGiJtrZ5WPQtAnBOy06yuxWnK/1a3aae5df5af54cd0c7d4bf29cf90b3752e565f1ea9933888635fd935ffbe388.png)

I made the firmware for QuickPad today, meaning I'm pretty much done designing! Firmware is definitely a strength of mine, so it didn't take nearly as long as designing hardware. I first had to update the Arduino IDE and download two libraries: Adafruit_SSD1306 for the OLED screen, and RTClib for the clock module.

For the keys, the code maps function keys 1-6 to its corresponding switch since my keyboard doesn't have any function keys. I also wrote the function checkKey() that "presses" a key for as long as its switch goes down.

I decided to have the rotary encoder control volume, so I programmed it so that turning it will adjust the volume. The rotary encoder also has a built-in switch, which I mapped to mute.

The OLED screen displays the date and time in an AM/PM format. I used a ternary operator to do that part, which I learned about in school. I think that my while mapping my PCB, I formatted the pins upside down, so I added a line of code that rotates the screen 180 degrees.

Finally, I worked on the clock module. As soon as I compile the code, the clock module will record the date and time and retain it, even when I unplug the board, thanks to its coin cell battery.

To finalize QuickPad, I uploaded all my files on GitHub and wrote a readme. I actually don't use GitHub that much, so I met up with a friend of mine and he helped me out. I used the Fabrication Toolkit tool in KiCad to make a production folder, then my friend helped me add the schematic and PCB design. I'm pretty proud of QuickPad and what I've learned and accomplished. Next week is CAD week, so I plan to design a cool case for it next!

![Screenshot 2026-10-10 at 7.55.22 PM](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/oWK9iPLBGiJtrZ5WPQtAnBOy06yuxWnK/50a757beb719d84a8a52eb8ab063b637e991a82f2e15facd0c4e0917d60157a3.png)

# TL;DR: I finished designing QuickPad! My firmware maps each switch to a function key, makes the rotary encoder control volume, and uses the clock module to display the date and time on the OLED screen. I then uploaded all my files to GitHub with my friend's help and wrote a readme.
